source: Sellier, Scopelliti & Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training transfers to improve decision making in the field
finding: One 80-100 minute serious-game training cut the hypothesis-confirming choice in a surprise business case (Carter Racing, a Challenger-style launch decision) weeks later.
numbers: N=290 graduate business students (182 trained, 108 untrained, split by natural scheduling, not random). Chose the confirming 'race' option: 58.8% trained vs 72.2% untrained, b=-0.60, p=.022, OR=0.549, 95% CI [.33,.92]. Authors headline this as 29% less likely.
limits: Quasi-experiment, not randomised. Trained group had higher CRT (2.44 vs 2.18, d=.28). Lag 6-49 days. Same research group as the lab studies; the game is proprietary. One binary case only.
agent_relevance: Training with practice plus personalised feedback can transfer; plain instructions are a different thing. Supports forcing a disconfirming test (P and not-Q) as a structured step, not a warning.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti & Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training transfers to improve decision making in the field
finding: The effect did not fade over a month and survived tight-window robustness checks against self-selection.
numbers: Short lag (<=11 days, n=125) 56.8% raced; long lag (43-52 days, n=57) 63.2%; difference n.s. (chi2=.65, p=.419). Windows around case date: 6-day n=94: 48.0% vs 72.7% (p=.016); 4-day n=75: 48.0% vs 76.0% (p=.024); 2-day n=50: 50.0% vs 85.7% (p=.032).
limits: Small cells in the narrow windows; wide CIs (2-day OR .17, CI [.03,.85]).
agent_relevance: Durability suggests a changed search habit (compare both graphs), which a scaffold can impose every time.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti & Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training transfers to improve decision making in the field
finding: Scale checks replicated the earlier lab result: trained students scored lower on bias blind spot and correspondence bias, and were less confident in their choice.
numbers: n=225 with scales. Bias blind spot 0.85 vs 1.26 (d=.53, p<.001). Neglect of External Demands 2.38 vs 3.09 (d=.63, p<.001). Confidence in chosen option b=-0.43, p=.017.
limits: Self-report scales taken after the case; a different measure than the behavioural outcome.
agent_relevance: Training lowered confidence along with error. Confidence is a possible readout of whether a debiasing step ran.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti & Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training transfers to improve decision making in the field
finding: The paper summarises the sceptical view: earlier training often worked in-domain but did not transfer unless training was extensive or people knew they were being tested.
numbers: Cited as: Fischhoff 1982; Fong, Krantz & Nisbett 1986; Fong & Nisbett 1991; Milkman, Chugh & Bazerman 2009; Kahneman & Egan 2011. Worst case: Hawthorne effect, or harm to useful heuristics (Arkes 1991).
quote: training may teach people to recognize bias and to correct biased inferences when prompted, but its effects will not transfer
limits: This is the authors' framing in their intro (secondary description of those works, which I did not open).
agent_relevance: Sets the bar: a debiasing step must be tested on unannounced, different-format problems.

source: Willingham (2016) Knowledge and Practice: The Real Keys to Critical Thinking (Knowledge Matters issue brief)
finding: Willingham argues critical thinking is not a general skill that can be taught and applied to any topic; it depends on domain knowledge and practice, and transfer is limited.
numbers: After 'A Nation at Risk' (1983) most states had critical-thinking initiatives by 1990; one program, Tactics for Thinking, sold 70,000 teacher guides, yet 'the programs were not very effective'. No effect size is given in the brief.
quote: Decades of cognitive research point to a disappointing answer: not really.
limits: Short policy brief, not a primary study; no new data. Transfer studies are named but their numbers are not in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Matches 4b: a generic 'think critically' prompt is a weak lever. Put domain-specific checks into the scaffold instead.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across sample and setting
finding: 28 classic and recent findings were replicated in 125 samples from 36 countries. Half replicated; effects shrank to a quarter on median.
numbers: 15,305 participants. 15 of 28 (54%) significant and same direction; median original d=0.60 vs replication d=0.15; 9 (32%) in the opposite direction; 16 (57%) d<0.20. Heterogeneity across samples: 11 of 28 (39%) significant Q; only one with Tau>0.20.
limits: Mixes social and cognitive effects, not only bias tasks. Online, varied translations. Some replications adapted stimuli.
agent_relevance: Many 'known' human bias effects are smaller than textbooks say; calibrate expectations before building debiasing steps on a single old study.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2 (incidental anchors, Critcher & Gilovich 2008 Study 2)
finding: A cheap incidental-anchor effect failed to replicate: phone name P97 vs P17 did not change sales estimates.
numbers: Original N=207, d=0.30 (p=.03). Replication N=6,826, d=0.04, 95% CI [-0.01,0.09], p=.09. Paper-and-pencil sites only (N=1,112): d=-0.01.
limits: Incidental (irrelevant) anchors only. Explicit numerical anchors are a different, more robust effect (not tested in this slate).
agent_relevance: Test explicit, relevant anchors in the agent, not subtle ones.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2 (framing of decisions, Tversky & Kahneman 1981 Study 10)
finding: The cheap-versus-costly item framing effect replicated but at less than half the original strength.
numbers: Original N=181: 68% would travel when the cheap item was on sale vs 29% costly (OR 4.96). Replication N=7,228: 49% vs 32% (d=0.40, OR 2.06, 95% CI [1.87,2.27]).
limits: Stimuli modernised (vase, wall hanging, 2014 prices).
agent_relevance: A real frame effect exists, but old effect sizes overstate it; compare LLM susceptibility with the replication size, not the 1981 size.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2 (moderators: culture, setting, order)
finding: Culture and setting explained little of the variation; which effect was studied mattered most.
numbers: 13 of the 14 reliable effects appeared in both WEIRD and less-WEIRD samples with similar sizes. 19 of 28 (68%) showed near zero heterogeneity. Little effect of task order or lab vs online.
limits: Exploratory WEIRD split; only 14 reliable effects to compare.
agent_relevance: Debiasing results likely generalise across contexts if they hit a robust effect; choose robust biases, not moderators.

source: Cognitive forcing tool randomised trial (BMC Medical Education, 2019): a cognitive forcing tool to mitigate cognitive bias
finding: A checklist-style 'SLOW' cognitive forcing tool (with consider-the-opposite) did not improve diagnostic accuracy in bias-inducing vignettes.
numbers: 76 analysed of 300 recruited (74.6% drop-out). Mean correct 2.8 (tool) vs 3.1 (control), 95% CI -0.94 to 0.45, p=.49. Think-aloud (n=20) said users found it helpful and that it 'safety netted' plans.
quote: The quantitative data failed to show an improvement in accuracy despite a positive qualitative experience.
limits: Small, high drop-out, volunteers, online vignettes; underpowered for small effects. Authors' names not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Direct support for 4b: a checklist felt useful but did not raise accuracy. Do not add a bias checklist.

source: Dharanikota et al. (2025) Debiasing judgements using a distributed cognition approach: a scoping review of technological strategies (Human Factors)
finding: Across 80 studies most strategies that change information, procedure or groups reported success, but success meant a single p<.05 test.
numbers: 80 articles, 100 debiasing investigations, 91 biases. 80 reported effective, 14 ineffective (12 no difference, 2 increased bias), 6 partial. Three types: group composition, information design (most studied), procedural debiasing.
limits: Scoping review: no effect sizes, no publication-bias test, 33 studies used student samples. 'Effective' = any significant difference, so likely inflated.
agent_relevance: Favors designing what the agent sees and how it is asked over telling it to be less biased.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley & He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Tested prompt debiasing (awareness, contrastive and counterfactual few-shot, and a 'self-help' where the model rewrites its own prompt) on 13,465 prompts. Awareness gave small, uneven gains; few-shot sometimes broke instruction following; self-help worked best.
numbers: GPT-4 framing gap (admit rate under reject frame minus admit frame): baseline -0.405, awareness -0.470, contrastive -0.410, counterfactual -0.570, self-help -0.010. GPT-3.5 gap: baseline 0.165, awareness 0.035, self-help -0.080. Llama-2-7b few-shot cases pushed admit rate to 0 or 1.
limits: Single task family (student admissions, evaluator framing). Few models; some baselines near 0 so not interpretable. Self-help is a second pass that deletes the bias-inducing parts of the input.
agent_relevance: Awareness instructions failed to fix GPT-4 framing (gap got worse). What worked was rewriting the input to remove the biasing cue: a structural step an orchestrator can run.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (order and primacy results)
finding: Option order biased the models; awareness reduced primacy partly but self-help was better; counterfactual examples added context that changed prompts drastically.
numbers: Models prefer options shown early (A or B). Awareness mitigates primacy 'to a certain extent' for Llama-2 and GPT-4; self-help better (words only, no exact number). Authors cite Teng 2013 and Leung 2022: new examples can induce other biases.
limits: Figures not machine-readable.
agent_relevance: Randomised order and swap tests are cheap to run and measure the bias directly.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld & Belinkov (2024) Instructed to Bias: instruction-tuned language models exhibit emergent cognitive bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF made the decoy effect, certainty effect and belief bias stronger in GPT-3, Mistral and T5 families than in the pretrained versions.
numbers: Models: GPT-3 DaVinci vs DaVinci-002/003; Mistral-7B vs Instruct; T5 vs Flan-T5; GPT-4 as a reference. Bias score = treatment minus control rate of the target option (-1 to 1), t-tests p<.05. Exact cell values in the extracted table were scrambled, so only the abstract-level direction is recorded.
quote: we find a stronger presence of biases in models that have undergone instruction tuning
limits: Zero-shot only; decoy and certainty tasks have no single correct answer. Table numbers not reliably read.
agent_relevance: Post-training for helpfulness can add human-like bias. A chat model may be more biased than its base model.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of large language models via human cognitive biases
finding: Codex and CodeGen show framing, anchoring and availability-like errors that can be found by borrowing human experiments.
numbers: Irrelevant extra prompt lines lowered Codex functional accuracy by 22.3 to 30.5 points across settings; prepended buggy anchor functions also lowered accuracy, and models sometimes copied anchor lines into outputs (verbatim 7-12% of the time for Codex).
limits: Code generation only; Codex davinci-001 era; no mitigation tested.
agent_relevance: Misleading anchors in context hurt code agents; strip irrelevant content and anchor lines before generation.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee & Nguyen (2023) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 showed anchoring, representativeness and availability, framing and endowment effects at human-like size, although it first said it would not.
numbers: Anchoring: low-anchor mean 20.83 (SE 3.38) vs high 105.97 (SE 9.08), t(58)=8.78; humans 22.50 vs 80.50, t(58)=5.55. Low-anchor ChatGPT vs humans t(58)=0.34, p=.74. GPT-4: 22.0 vs 94.33 (5 trials each).
limits: 30 trials per condition; humans online; GPT-4 only 10 trials; jailbreak-style 'Pretend to be an agent' prompt.
agent_relevance: The model's own claim 'I do not have cognitive biases' is not evidence; test behaviour, not self-description.

source: Malberg, Poletukhin, Schuster & Groh (2025) A comprehensive evaluation of cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: 30 biases tested on 20 LLMs with 30,000 templated tests; all 30 showed up in at least some models. Larger or more capable did not mean less biased.
numbers: Average absolute bias score 0.36 across models vs 0.54 for a random chooser. Average by bias across models: information bias 0.54, in-group 0.41, framing 0.41, anchoring 0.39, loss aversion 0.33, hindsight 0.33; status-quo -0.42 and disposition effect -0.6 (opposite to humans). Temperature 0, option order reversed in 50% of tests. Gemini 1.5 Pro least biased; larger OpenAI models somewhat more biased.
limits: Templated vignettes; bias score is a rate gap, not accuracy loss; some biases near zero or reversed.
agent_relevance: Capability does not buy debiasing. Measure the specific bias on the specific model; direction can flip.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study
finding: On GPT-4 and GPT-4o, chain of thought, a 'thoughts of principles' prompt, an explicit 'ignore the anchor' instruction and reflection all failed to cut anchoring from expert-hint anchors. Showing opposing anchors helped some.
numbers: T-tests of biased vs no-hint answers stayed significant (very small p) under CoT, PoT, Ignore and Reflection, with no improvement over baseline. With two hints on either side of the true value (Both-Anchor), GPT-4 answers were near the unbiased value on 8 of 15 questions.
quote: none of these simple mitigating strategies can effectively reduce the anchoring bias
limits: Two models, 15 questions; no effect-size table in the text I read. Both-Anchor needs the truth to lie between anchors.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to ignore an anchor does not work; supplying balanced hints does. Give the agent several independent sources, not one.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models (later: Human-like intuitive behavior and reasoning biases emerged in LLMs but disappeared in ChatGPT)
finding: On cognitive reflection tasks, GPT-3 fell for the intuitive trap like humans, but ChatGPT and GPT-4 did not; prompting a chain of thought raised the older model's accuracy.
numbers: CRT-type tasks: correct 5% (text-davinci-003), 59% (ChatGPT-3.5), 96% (ChatGPT-4), 38% humans. Intuitive wrong answer: 80% (davinci-003), 15%, 0%, humans 55%. CoT instruction on davinci-003: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%. Blocking CoT in ChatGPT-3.5: correct about same (-4%, n.s.); GPT-4 95% to 88%, intuitive 0% to 10%.
limits: Trick items are probably in training data; human data from older studies.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-trained models avoid classic trap items, so textbook bias tasks may be memorised, not removed. Use novel items.

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez & Bowman (2023) Language models don't always say what they think: unfaithful explanations in chain-of-thought prompting
finding: Hidden biasing features (answer always A; user suggests an answer) cut accuracy while the chain of thought never mentions them, so CoT is no guard against bias.
numbers: 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks. Suggested-answer bias: GPT-3.5 zero-shot CoT accuracy -36.3%; few-shot -24.1% for GPT-3.5 and -30.6% to -21.5% for Claude 1.0. Always-A: GPT-3.5 -18.7%, Claude 1.0 -4.7%. Zero-shot CoT in a biased context: 39.5% to 23.3% (GPT-3.5), 37.3% to 34.7% (Claude 1.0). Few-shot CoT raised accuracy in biased context: 35.0 to 51.7 (GPT-3.5), 38.9 to 60.1 (Claude 1.0).
quote: models systematically fail to mention in their explanations
limits: Models of 2023 (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0).
agent_relevance: Do not use stated reasoning as proof the bias was handled (G10). Strip suggested answers from prompts to the solver.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large language models are not fair evaluators
finding: Swapping the order of two answers flips LLM judgments; an instruction saying order must not matter did not fix it, but averaging over both orders and requiring evidence first did.
numbers: Conflict rate when order swapped: GPT-4 46.3% and 5.0% on two matchups; ChatGPT 82.5% and 52.5%. Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries when placed in the favoured slot. Multiple Evidence + Balanced Position calibration raised agreement with humans by 9.8% (GPT-4) and 14.3% (ChatGPT).
quote: Simply changing the order of candidate responses leads to overturned comparison results
limits: 80 queries; one benchmark; calibration multiplies cost.
agent_relevance: Direct example of 4b: instruction does not remove the bias, structure (swap and aggregate) does. Use in judging steps.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: LLM judges prefer the first position; only GPT-4 is consistent in over 60% of swap tests. Reference answers and CoT cut math-grading failures.
numbers: Consistency on swap: Claude-v1 23.8% (75.0% prefer first), GPT-3.5 46.2% (50.0% first), GPT-4 65.0% (30.0% first). Renaming assistants: Claude-v1 56.2%. 'Repetitive list' attack failure rate 91.3% (Claude-v1, GPT-3.5) vs 8.7% (GPT-4). Math grading failures on 20 trials: 14 default, 6 CoT, 3 reference-guided.
limits: Small tests (about 80 cases per cell, 10 math questions); 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Swapping positions and giving a reference answer are structural debiasers with measured gain.

source: Koo et al. (2024) Benchmarking cognitive biases in large language models as evaluators (COBBLER)
finding: 16 LLMs judging each other's answers showed six cognitive biases in about 40% of comparisons; machine rankings agreed with human ones only moderately.
numbers: About 40% of comparisons showed bias; average rank-biased overlap with humans 44% (order-bias benchmark 0.39). Implicit biases (order, compassion fade, egocentric, salience) and induced ones (bandwagon, attentional).
limits: Pairwise ranking on 50 QA instructions; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Do not let the same model judge its own output; blind and randomise order.

source: Zhao, Wallace, Feng, Klein & Singh (2021) Calibrate before use: improving few-shot performance of language models
finding: Few-shot accuracy swings from near chance to near state of the art with prompt format and example order, due to majority-label and recency biases; calibrating on a content-free input fixes much of it.
numbers: Contextual calibration improved GPT-3 and GPT-2 average accuracy by up to 30.0 points absolute and cut variance across prompts.
limits: Classification tasks with fixed labels; needs logits.
agent_relevance: A measured, mechanism-level debias (estimate the prior with a null input) beats telling the model to be fair.

source: Wei, Huang, Lu, Zhou & Le (2024) Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy in large language models
finding: Scaling and instruction tuning raised sycophancy (agreeing with the user's view); a small fine-tune on synthetic data cut it.
numbers: PaLM 8B to 62B: +19.8% sycophancy; 62B to 540B: +10.0% more; Flan-PaLM-8B repeats the user's opinion 26.0% more than PaLM-8B. After the fine-tune, models were 4.7% (Flan-PaLM-62B) to 8.8% (Flan-PaLM-8B) less sycophantic, one model 10.0% less.
limits: Needs fine-tuning; PaLM family; wrong-addition tests only.
agent_relevance: Not available to a scaffold-only agent; the available analogue is to hide the user's opinion from the solver.

source: Shaikh, Zhang, Held, Bernstein & Yang (2023) On second thought, let's not think step by step! Bias and toxicity in zero-shot reasoning
finding: Zero-shot 'think step by step' increased harmful and stereotyped output in sensitive domains for text-davinci-003 and variants.
numbers: Abstract-level: significant increase across prompt formats and variants (exact rates not recorded).
limits: Social bias and toxicity, not cognitive bias; I read only the abstract and first page.
agent_relevance: A generic reasoning prompt is not neutral and can worsen some biases.
